Follow the protein and the display molecule separately. In direct/endogenous presentation, the presenting cell makes the protein and uses its own class-I HLA. In cross-presentation, it acquires protein from another source, processes it and displays a fragment on its own HLA. In cross-dressing, it acquires an intact peptide-HLA complex from a donor surface, retaining the donor-associated display molecule. That starting point does not specify where the donor's peptide originally came from or how it was generated. This comparison tracks provenance, rather than one intracellular itinerary, physical transfer mechanism or activation outcome. Wakim and Bevan demonstrated transferred peptide-MHC complexes in a mouse viral model; this does not establish the same mechanism in every human setting.

Material uptake is not a display assay. Supplied peptide can load display molecules without demonstrating recipient processing of an external protein. Track donor and recipient HLA, the acquired material, target-specific display or responder results and suitable backgrounds. In a fictional experiment, a dendritic cell engulfs tumour debris and displays a tumour-derived class-I peptide; this supports cross-presentation. Without a naive T-cell activation measurement, cross-priming remains untested, as do downstream tumour killing and patient benefit. A cell marker alone cannot settle the question: in Jongbloed's defined human assays, both CD141-positive and CD1c-positive cells cross-presented soluble pp65, whereas only CD141-positive cells cross-presented the tested necrotic-cell antigen. The soluble-protein result also depended on stimulation conditions. These are antigen- and condition-specific findings, rather than a universal CD141 functional test.
